stories.headline: Update: Trump Declares Iran Ceasefire 'Over' After U.S. Strikes 80 Targets; Supreme Court Upholds Birthright Citizenship
stories.summary:
President Trump declared the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding effectively dead on Wednesday, saying "to me, I think it's over" after the U.S. military struck more than 80 Iranian targets overnight — including missile, drone, and port facilities — in retaliation for Iranian attacks on three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump, speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara, called Iranian leadership "scum" and said negotiations were "a waste of time," while oil prices surged more than 5% on news that the U.S. had also revoked a sanctions waiver allowing Iranian oil sales. Iran threatened a "crushing response" and said it had already struck U.S. military sites in the Gulf.

The escalation marks a sharp reversal from the ceasefire Trump had described weeks ago as Iran's "unconditional surrender." Both sides have accused each other of violating the memorandum of understanding. The exchange of fire risks plunging the two countries into a renewed cycle of retaliation and threatens global energy supplies flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for world oil markets.

Separately, the U.S. Supreme Court issued its most consequential ruling of the term on the same day, striking down Trump's executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship and upholding the longstanding constitutional guarantee. The 6-3 conservative court's decision was a major defeat for the administration's immigration agenda, though Trump immediately signaled he would pursue legislative alternatives, creating new headaches for congressional Republican leaders.

The court also ruled that states may ban transgender athletes from competing in female school and college sports, finding that such restrictions do not violate Title IX — a ruling cheered by Republican-led states and criticized by civil rights advocates as discriminatory. The twin decisions capped a high-stakes Supreme Court term with sweeping implications for immigration law, civil rights, and the limits of executive power.

stories.headline: Update: Succession Battle Underway in Maine as Democrats Pressure Platner to Exit Senate Race
stories.summary:
Maine Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner has not withdrawn from the race despite mounting calls from prominent party figures, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Senators Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, and dozens of others, who have urged him to step aside following a rape allegation from a former girlfriend. Platner denies all allegations, but a second woman has also accused him of removing condoms during sex without her consent, according to The Washington Post. The Maine Democratic Party's executive director said Tuesday that the party is developing a replacement process but will not disclose details until Platner formally withdraws.

The stakes are high: Maine was considered Democrats' best opportunity to flip a Senate seat and potentially regain the majority. Platner has until July 13 to withdraw and allow the state party to select a replacement nominee to face incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Multiple potential replacements have already begun positioning themselves, and Republicans have reportedly prepared $8 million in negative ads ready to deploy against whoever emerges as a new Democratic candidate.

The Maine Democratic Party executive director said Platner's campaign has repeatedly attempted to influence the replacement process, a claim the campaign disputes. Democrats nationally are scrambling to manage the fallout, with the episode exposing tensions over vetting and candidate selection within the party just four months before Election Day.

The situation presents a stark contrast in how each party is responding: Republicans are already preparing to capitalize, while Democrats remain divided over the pace and process of replacing their nominee. Platner, who won the primary in June, has called the rape allegation "categorically false" and says thousands of Maine voters who supported him deserve a voice in what comes next.

stories.headline: Typhoon Maysak Kills 17, Displaces Tens of Thousands Across Southern China
stories.summary:
Typhoon Maysak swept through China's southern Guangxi province over the weekend and into Monday, causing rivers to overflow, dam walls to break, and flooding that has inundated the regional capital Nanning and surrounding villages. At least 17 people have died, hundreds more have been injured, and roughly 90,000 people are affected, with state media reporting that 60,000 have been evacuated. Residents described floodwaters rising from knee height to submerging entire first floors within hours, with many families trapped on rooftops and cut off from communication.

The typhoon also triggered thunderstorms and rare tornadoes hundreds of kilometers away in Hubei province, compounding the death toll. President Xi Jinping has ordered "all-out" rescue and relief operations, but local residents told the BBC that too few rescue personnel and inadequate equipment have left thousands stranded, including a four-month-old infant without milk for more than a day.

Authorities in Nanning warned that continued heavy rain could hamper ongoing rescue efforts. A second powerful storm, Super Typhoon Bavi, is now churning across the Pacific and is forecast to strike China's eastern coast later this week, raising the prospect of additional catastrophic flooding before the current disaster is resolved.

stories.headline: Hungary's New Government Suspends State Broadcaster News Programs, Ends Orban-Era Propaganda
stories.summary:
Hungary's main public television channel M1 halted its news broadcasts Tuesday and state radio station Kossuth was suspended entirely, as Prime Minister Péter Magyar's new government moved to dismantle what it described as years of government propaganda under ousted former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. M1 displayed a message on screen reading: "Public media should not lie. We are sorry for doing it for so long," and pledged to relaunch with an independent editorial team. Magyar called the day "historic" and said it marked "the end of propaganda broadcasts on public media platforms."

Orbán, who was removed from power in April after 16 years, condemned the move on Facebook as "Tisza party tyranny" — referring to Magyar's ruling party — and directed supporters to watch Fidesz-affiliated Hir TV instead. Magyar had promised sweeping media reform during his campaign, saying a majority of Hungarian media had been captured by Orbán allies who blocked him from appearing on state television for years.

The suspension of Hungary's flagship public broadcaster represents one of the most visible steps yet in Magyar's "regime change" agenda and carries significance for the European Union, which had long criticized Orbán's media controls. The EU previously unlocked €16.4 billion in frozen funds after Magyar's election, citing Hungary's democratic trajectory.
